concepts.name: Definition and Mathematical Threshold of Special Majority under Article 368
key_dimensions: Dual requirement: majority of total membership AND 2/3rd majority of members present and voting — both must be satisfied simultaneously
UPSC trap: distinction between 'total membership' (fixed strength) vs 'members present and voting' (variable quorum-based count)
Comparison with simple majority (Article 100) and absolute majority — where each applies
Practical scenario: if 400 out of 545 Lok Sabha members are present, calculating the threshold for special majority

concepts.name: Scope of Articles Amendable by Special Majority Only (No Ratification Required)
key_dimensions: Categories covered: Fundamental Rights (Part III), Directive Principles (Part IV), all provisions NOT listed under ratification requirement
UPSC trap: conflating 'special majority' articles with 'special majority + ratification' articles — the default amendment route is special majority alone
Examples: Articles 19, 21, 32, 44 — amendable by special majority without state ratification
Judicial overlay: Basic Structure doctrine limits Parliament's power even when procedural requirements are met

concepts.name: Article 368: Structure, Scope, and Limitations
key_dimensions: Article 368(1): power of Parliament to amend AND procedure thereof — both vested in Parliament
Article 368(2): special majority procedure detailed; proviso lists ratification-required provisions
Article 368(3) added by 24th CAA 1971: President shall give assent — made mandatory, removing discretion
UPSC trap: Article 368 itself is amendable by special majority (not ratification) — confirmed in Kesavananda Bharati

concepts.name: Initiation of Amendment Bill: Parliament's Exclusive Power
key_dimensions: Amendment bill can be introduced in EITHER House of Parliament — unlike Money Bills which must originate in Lok Sabha
UPSC trap: Amendment bills cannot be introduced in State Legislatures; states can only ratify, not initiate
Amendment bills can be introduced by any member (not necessarily a minister) — unlike Money Bills requiring recommendation of President
No joint sitting provision for deadlock on Constitution Amendment Bills — distinguished from ordinary bills under Article 108

concepts.name: Role of President in Constitutional Amendment: Article 368(2) vs Article 111
key_dimensions: Post-24th CAA: President MUST give assent — has no power to withhold or return a Constitution Amendment Bill
UPSC trap: contrast with ordinary bills (Article 111) where President can withhold assent or return for reconsideration
Pre-24th CAA position: President's assent was not explicitly mandated — Shankari Prasad case background
24th CAA constitutionality upheld in Kesavananda Bharati — making presidential assent mandatory is valid

concepts.name: Fundamental Rights Amendability: Evolution through Judicial Pronouncements
key_dimensions: Shankari Prasad (1951): Fundamental Rights can be amended under Article 368 — 'law' in Article 13 doesn't include constitutional amendments
Sajjan Singh (1965): Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad — Parliament has constituent power to amend FR
Golaknath (1967): Overruled — FRs cannot be abridged/taken away; Parliament has no power; prospective overruling applied
24th CAA (1971) + Kesavananda Bharati (1973): FRs CAN be amended but subject to Basic Structure — current settled position

concepts.name: Basic Structure Doctrine as an Implied Limitation on Special Majority Power
key_dimensions: Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Even with special majority, Parliament cannot destroy Basic Structure of Constitution
UPSC trap: Basic Structure is NOT written in the Constitution — it is a judicially evolved doctrine limiting Article 368 power
Key elements held as Basic Structure: Supremacy of Constitution, Judicial Review, Federalism, Secularism, Free & Fair Elections
Minerva Mills (1980): Added that limited amending power itself is part of Basic Structure — Articles 368(4) and 368(5) struck down

concepts.name: 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976: Overreach and Judicial Correction
key_dimensions: Added clauses 368(4) and 368(5): declared amendments immune from judicial review and Parliament has unlimited constituent power
Minerva Mills (1980): Struck down both clauses — judicial review of amendments is part of Basic Structure
42nd CAA also amended Preamble (Socialist, Secular, Integrity added) — this amendment to Preamble via special majority upheld
UPSC trap: 42nd CAA attempted to make special majority omnipotent — courts curtailed this; demonstrates limits of procedure

concepts.name: Amendment of Fundamental Rights vs Amendment of Article 13 Itself
key_dimensions: Article 13(2): State shall not make law abridging Fundamental Rights — 'law' defined in Article 13(3)
Core debate: Does 'law' in Article 13 include a Constitutional Amendment Act? — Shankari Prasad said NO, Golaknath said YES
Post-Kesavananda settled position: Constitutional amendments are NOT 'law' under Article 13, but Basic Structure limits persist
UPSC trap: Article 13 itself (being in Part III) is amendable by special majority, but amendment cannot destroy the right to equality framework if it's Basic Structure

concepts.name: Special Majority Requirement: Joint Sitting Exception and Its Absence
key_dimensions: Article 108 joint sitting applies ONLY to ordinary bills — not to Constitution Amendment Bills
UPSC trap: If Rajya Sabha rejects or passes with amendments a Constitution Amendment Bill, there is NO provision for joint sitting — the bill lapses or deadlock continues
This gives Rajya Sabha effective veto power over constitutional amendments — strengthens federal character
Contrast: Money Bill — Rajya Sabha has limited role; Ordinary Bill — joint sitting possible; Amendment Bill — Rajya Sabha has equal and absolute power

concepts.name: Special Majority in Both Houses Independently: No Provision for Lapsing on Dissolution
key_dimensions: Each House must independently pass the bill with special majority — there is no concept of one House 'sending it' to the other as in ordinary bills
UPSC trap: Unlike ordinary bills, there is ambiguity on whether Constitution Amendment Bills lapse on dissolution of Lok Sabha — conventionally treated as lapsing
Amendment bills passed by one House but pending in another — both Houses must pass in the SAME or different sessions (no time limit specified in Article 368)
Comparison: Ordinary bills lapse on dissolution; Money bills passed by Lok Sabha are deemed passed after 14 days even if RS doesn't act

concepts.name: Preamble: Amendability by Special Majority and Basic Structure Constraints
key_dimensions: Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Preamble is part of the Constitution and CAN be amended under Article 368
42nd CAA 1976: Added 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' — done by special majority, upheld as valid
UPSC trap: Core elements of Preamble (Sovereignty, Democratic Republic, Justice, Liberty, Equality) are themselves part of Basic Structure — cannot be abridged
Berubari Union Case (1960): Preamble is NOT part of Constitution (pre-Kesavananda position) — important for evolution question

concepts.name: Amendment of Part III (Fundamental Rights): Specific Articles and Special Majority Nuances
key_dimensions: Right to Property (Article 31) deleted by 44th CAA 1978 via special majority — moved to Article 300A as a legal right (not fundamental right)
UPSC trap: Deletion of a Fundamental Right requires only special majority (not ratification) but is subject to Basic Structure scrutiny
Article 31A, 31B (Ninth Schedule), 31C: Added/amended by special majority — Ninth Schedule laws were shielded from judicial review until I.R. Coelho (2007)
I.R. Coelho (2007): Laws added to Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are subject to Basic Structure/FR review — special majority not sufficient protection

concepts.name: Amendment of Directive Principles and its Interplay with Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: DPSPs (Part IV) are amendable by special majority — no ratification needed
25th CAA 1971: Added Article 31C — laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) cannot be challenged under Articles 14 and 19
Kesavananda upheld Article 31C partially; Minerva Mills struck down its extension to ALL DPSPs — only Articles 39(b)(c) covered
UPSC trap: After 42nd CAA extended Article 31C to all DPSPs, Minerva Mills curtailed it — creating a specific hierarchy between FRs and DPSPs in amendment context

concepts.name: Ninth Schedule: Addition of Laws via Special Majority and Judicial Review
key_dimensions: Ninth Schedule created by 1st CAA 1951 — laws placed here were immune from FR challenge under Article 31B
Adding a law to Ninth Schedule requires a Constitutional Amendment Act passed by special majority
UPSC trap: The ACT of placing a law in Ninth Schedule requires special majority, but the law itself may have been passed by simple majority in a legislature
I.R. Coelho (2007): Post-April 24, 1973 Ninth Schedule entries can be judicially reviewed — special majority placement does not guarantee immunity if Basic Structure violated

concepts.name: Amendment of Chapter IV-A (Fundamental Duties, Article 51A): Special Majority Sufficiency
key_dimensions: Article 51A added by 42nd CAA 1976 — required only special majority (not ratification) as it does not fall under proviso to Article 368(2)
UPSC trap: Fundamental Duties are in Part IV-A — not Part III or Part IV — so their amendment requires only special majority, confirming the 'default = special majority' rule
No judicial enforcement mechanism for FDs — amendment to add/remove duties via special majority alone
Verma Committee (1999) recommended making some FDs legally enforceable — if done, would require special majority amendment

concepts.name: Special Majority vs. Ordinary Majority: UPSC Trap Zones in Specific Provisions
key_dimensions: UPSC trap: Some provisions APPEAR federal/important but require only simple majority — e.g., creation of new states (Article 3), abolition of Legislative Councils (Article 169)
Counter-trap: Some provisions require special majority but are often forgotten — e.g., amendment of Article 368 itself, amendment of election to Parliament (Article 327 vs 324)
Article 169: Abolition/creation of State Legislative Councils needs only simple majority in Parliament + resolution by state legislature — NOT special majority
Distinguishing marker: If a provision explicitly says 'notwithstanding Article 368' or falls in proviso — ratification needed; otherwise special majority is sufficient and default

concepts.name: Amendment of Emergency Provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) via Special Majority
key_dimensions: National Emergency (Art 352), President's Rule (Art 356), Financial Emergency (Art 360) — amendable by special majority without state ratification
UPSC trap: The PROCLAMATION of Emergency requires special majority for approval (Article 352(6)) — this is an operational requirement, NOT an amendment procedure
44th CAA 1978 amended Article 352 — changed 'internal disturbance' to 'armed rebellion', added safeguards — done by special majority only

Distinction: Amending the Article (constitutional change via Art 368 special majority) vs. Approving a Proclamation (parliamentary approval via special majority under Art 352) — two different special majorities for different purposes

concepts.name: Constitutional Amendments Affecting Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule) via Special Majority
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule added by 52nd CAA 1985 — required special majority (not ratification) as it relates to parliamentary membership, not federal structure
UPSC trap: Tenth Schedule amended Parliament's own composition rules — yet no state ratification needed, confirming non-federal nature of anti-defection provisions
91st CAA 2003 amended Tenth Schedule (size of Council of Ministers, defection rules) — special majority sufficient
Kihoto Hollohan (1992): Paragraph 7 of Tenth Schedule (barring court jurisdiction) struck down — even special majority cannot oust judicial review if it violates Basic Structure

concepts.name: Reservation-Related Constitutional Amendments via Special Majority: 77th to 85th CAAs
key_dimensions: 77th CAA 1995: Added Article 16(4A) — reservation in promotion for SC/STs — special majority only, no ratification
81st CAA 2000: Unfilled SC/ST vacancies carried forward — not counted in 50% ceiling (M. Nagaraj context)
UPSC trap: All reservation-related amendments to Part III (Article 15, 16) require only special majority — they amend Fundamental Rights but don't require state ratification

M. Nagaraj (2006) and Jarnail Singh (2018): Upheld these amendments but added 'compelling reasons, backwardness, inadequacy of representation' conditions — judicial limits on special majority power in reservation context
